#2067. Everton dispatch Newcastle to give Matthias Jaissle a reality check

Everton appear well ahead of Newcastle United in their preparation for the new Premier League season after a comfortable 3-1 victory at Murrayfield.

On a sobering evening for new Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle, who changed all 10 outfield players at half-time, Everton’s one and two-touch attacking play proved difficult to contain.

Everton took the lead through Thierno Barry after a defensive error from Sven Botman, before Iliman Ndiaye scored a penalty that was won cheaply by summer signing Hayden Hackney.

Newcastle’s raft of half-time changes helped David Moyes’s team strengthen their grip further, with Tyrique George adding a stylish third and 19-year-old Harrison Armstrong providing his second assist of the game.

Among the Newcastle players introduced at half-time was 18-year-old Sean Steur, the exciting midfield prospect signed from Ajax this summer. Aladji Bamba and Bazoumana Toure also flickered with promise, but a sharp start from Jaissle’s team faded.

They pulled a goal back late on when Jacob Murphy’s cross found Harvey Barnes at the back post, but they offered little as an attacking force throughout the second half.

Newcastle have two more friendlies, against Bayer Leverkusen and Strasbourg, before they begin their Premier League season at home to Liverpool.

The club are reeling from the summer departures of Bruno Guimaraes, Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and manager Eddie Howe, but David Hopkinson, the chief executive, struck a bullish tone when he spoke of this being the start of “Newcastle 2.0”.

Everton look the more settled side and club, and the performances of new arrivals Hackney and George were encouraging, while Thierno Barry was sharp in the centre-forward position that has proved so difficult for the club to fill in recent seasons.

Everton kick-off their new season at home to Crystal Palace, and keeping Ndiaye at the club beyond the end of the transfer window will be a priority.

The scoreline is a fair reflection of the game. Everton looked sharper, as well as fitter, and there are more positives for them to take. They look ready for the new season, Newcastle need reinforcements.

Alcaraz bends a shot not far wide from 25 yards for Everton. The game is meandering towards its conclusion now.

Willock collects the ball between the lines, feeds Murphy wide right, and his ball across goal is turned in at the back post by Harvey Barnes.

Moyes makes another pair of changes: Keane and Hackney off, O’Brien and Foster on.

Everton fans are enjoying themselves now, belting out Spirit of the Blues at Murrayfield.

More defending for Newcastle to do but they deal with Hackney’s corner delivery. All too easy for Everton to slice through their midfield in the build up though.

That goal had been coming, and Tyrique George is heavily involved again. He carries the ball forward and finds Armstrong, who returns the favour. George shoots on the swivel and picks out the bottom corner.

If I were a Newcastle fan in the stands, Edinbugh’s city centre hostelries would be looking very alluring just about now. There is not much for them to watch in this season half, they are chasing shadows. Some of that can be put down to the handful of young plyers in their second-half XI.

Tyler Dribbling drops a shoulder down the right, and wins a corner off Harvey Barnes. Everton are finishing this game the stronger, there are more goals in this should they put their foot on the pedal.

Newcastle, with some youngsters in their defence, looking a little ragged against Everton’s direct attacks now, but George runs into traffic at the edge of the box. Then Alcaraz is booked for a cynical foul.

Three more Everton changes on the way: Beto, Dibling and Alcaraz on for Barry, Ndiaye and Dewsbury-Hall.

Hayden Hackney plays a one-two with Tyrique George for Everton, with the former Chelsea winger backheeling the ball into Hackney’s path, and there were unheeded calls for a penalty. It was more of a penalty than the one Everton were awarded in the first half, Lewis Miley tripped him.

Thierno Barry’s performance has been a positive for Everton, could he nail down the No 9 role this season? It has been a problem position for several seasons now. Barry is tripped and Everton have a free-kick.

Dewsbury-Hall almost sneaks a shot in at the near post, but Hornicek tips the ball around the post.

Joe Willock with what was very nearly an exquisite disguised pass, but the flag was up for offside against Jacob Murphy.

Then an amusing moment: great cheers from the crowd as David Moyes heads a Hornicek clearance back down the line. He didn’t fancy the cushioned first touch off his instep, then.

Everton have played some quick one and two-touch football around the box in this game, and another move ends with George shooting over the bar. Everton are making their first change: Patterson off, replaced by Rohl.

The game is still finding its shape again after all those Newcastle changes, but Murphy did force a sharp save from Travers with a low shot from a tight angle.

He keeps to his word from before the game; Hornicek is the only player still on the pitch.

The players on for Newcastle are: Woltemade, Murphy, Willock, Barnes, Ramsey, Johnson, Steur, Pivas, Miley and Charlton.

It looks like an unchanged team from David Moyes, so Everton have a significantly more mature team on the pitch now.

Newcastle made a bright start, but as the half progressed there is no doubt that Everton have been the more dangerous attacking force and the scoreline reflects that. Here come the changes...

Everton have a late corner to defend, after another burst forward from Newcastle’s left-winger Toure. Newcastle try one off the training ground but the ball is cleared.

Thierno Barry almost finds the run of Hackney into the Newcastle penalty, and after a sluggish start, Everton have played some slick football in the attacking third.

A sign of some Newcastle frustration there was Wissa kicks Tyrique George across the shins. A bit naughty that, may even have been worthy of VAR attention in a Premier League game.

The Senegalese sends Hornicek the wrong way and finds the corner. No chance it was a penalty in the first place though, thankfully this is not a competitive game.

This is very soft, there was not much of a challenge by Joelinton on Dewsbury-Hall, but the Everton midfielder goes down in the box and is awarded the penalty.

It really should be 2-0 to Everton, a high-class moving down their left with Armstrong dinking a pass to Barry. He squared to Ndiaye who was free as a bird in the middle, but his shot was too close to Hornicek.

Joelinton runs down a blind alley before lumping a pass out for an Everton throw, and then the Newcastle man fouls Barry. The big Brazilian still finding his legs and getting up to speed.

A moment to forget for both Newcastle centre-backs. Thiaw was bumped and unbalance by Barry, before Botman steps out of defence and kicks fresh air against the Everton forward. Great recovery from Lewis Hall, but the ball breaks for Armstrong, who feeds Barry and he finishes across Hornicek.

Ndiaye has had a quiet start to the game for Everton, but his jinking qualities were on display there to beat a couple of Newcastle defenders. Everton lose the ball in midfield, and Tarkowski makes a superb last-ditch tackle to deny Osula.

Half-hearted appeals for a penalty from Wissa, but Hayden Hackney did not do much wrong. Looks like we will be spared a first-half hydration break, despite it being a sultry evening.

Osula skips through a couple of challenges at the edge of the area but fails to pick a pass in the box. Bazoumana Touré has looked lively for Newcastle on their left flank, and Bamba has done well for them in midfield.

Everton shake themselves into life as an attacking force. Cracking cross from Patterson into the box and Dewsbury-Hall’s run had gone untracked, but he was just stretching and could not generate enough power to beat Hornicek.

Good save from Travers to deny Elanga, but it was Mykolenko who made a hash of things in the box. The left back simply fell over the ball under no pressure. Newcastle the sharper of the two teams so far.

Joelinton feeds Bamba down the left wing for Newcastle who delivers a cross into the penalty area. Keane can only direct his defensive header back towards the penalty spot, but Wissa volleyed over with a first-time hit. Decent chance.

Thierno Barry makes it stick and proves a strong outlet for Everton. Botman brings him down at the expense of a free-kick just beyond the halfway line. Then Wissa drives into the penalty area for Newcastle after a one-two but he fouls Patterson.

Newcastle, playing in their lilac away kit, are the team trying to take the initiative with the ball, but Everton are quite happy staying compact and absorbing pressure. Elanga’s corner delivery is promising, but Osula does not connect cleanly at the back post.

Newcastle’s defenders enjoying comfortable possession in the early stages, Everton sitting off in their 4-4-2 defensive shape.

Wissa peels behind Everton’s defence inside the opening 90 seconds but he cannot lift the ball over Travers.

Bagpipes greet the players at Murrayfield, where the pitch has been reconfigured for football. There are only fans in the lower tier, and still plenty of empty seats even so.

We know it is a time in the pre-season when the legs are not that fresh, we train very intense but we want to play with an idea of how we want to play football. Intense with a vertical approach for sure, everyone gets 45 minutes except the goalkeeper.

Big Dunc and Moyes catch up pre-match! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/Jh4APHOZvX

A word that keeps being used about Jaissle is “special”. Newcastle’s hierarchy believe they have secured the services of a manager who will soon be recognised in the elite tier of European managers. We shall see how this view of the 38-year-old survives contact with a brutal and relentless Premier League campaign.

Newcastle XI: Hornicek; Shahar, Thiaw, Botman, Hall; Joelinton, Bamba; Elanga, Wissa, Toure; Osula

Newcastle subs: Gillespie, Harris, Charlton, Pivas, Johnson, M Miley, Finneran, Ramsey, Steur, Willock, J Murphy, Barnes, Neave, Woltemade

Your Mags at Murrayfield! ✊ pic.twitter.com/rDXpn0MqCg

Everton XI: Travers; Patterson, Tarkowski, Keane, Mykolenko; Hackney, Deswbury-Hall, Armstrong, Ndiaye; George, Barry

Here's how we start against Newcastle. UTT! 🔵📺 https://t.co/2VsWpyRq02 pic.twitter.com/vpnLPTRmLl

Newcastle United manager ​Matthias Jaissle is ‌refusing to dwell on the departure of key players that has left his club in turmoil going into the new season, as they step up their preparations against Everton at Murrayfield this evening.

Jaissle was recruited from Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli after Eddie Howe left last month, with the German coach joining a club who have lost Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and captain Bruno Guimaraes in quick succession.

“It’s a challenge, a big challenge, always when there’s a transitional period. ‌But it’s ‌not time to ⁠complain, it doesn’t make sense to see the negative things,” Jaissle said.

“We want to see the chance in that situation and that’s our approach from day one. We are here to do our ⁠best job. We want to support the players, the current squad.

“There will be adjustments to see in the coming days, weeks. But for now it’s only focused on the daily work, the work we can influence. That’s all that ​matters now.”

The 38-year-old coach arrived in Newcastle ‌having won two Austrian Bundesliga titles with Red Bull Salzburg before leading Al-Ahli to back-to-back AFC Champions League crowns.

He remained tight-lipped about new signings.

“Obviously, in that transition phase, the players who left the club were ‌great ​players, great characters, experienced ⁠players. This is now a vacuum,” he said.

“Either we adjust something in the squad, by signing these players, these profiles, or other players ⁠need to step up and fill ​these positions, these leadership roles. I’m quite optimistic, we can work in both scenarios.”

Jaissle said he had a ​clear vision of how he wants his team to play.

“The phrase how Newcastle ‌should play like is front-footed, intense, ​aggressive and of course also successful. ​In the end, it’s all about what ⁠I can ⁠say and it’s also why I’m sitting here,” he said.

“The approach we have as a coaching team and the identity of Newcastle is famed for, it’s so linked so close together - which is a perfect fit in my eyes and ​that’s going to be exciting.”

#2066. New twist in Ernie Weaver’s situation as Sheffield Wednesday revive National League loan plan

Sheffield Wednesday prospect Ernie Weaver has made a positive impression when selected for first-team football, but the depth at centre-back means there has been regular talk over a potential loan exit. Injuries changed plans previously, but now, the SWFC talent is now set to head out.

Reporting for The Wednesday Word, Joe Crann states that Weaver is not in Dave Challinor’s immediate plans and a temporary move will be sanctioned. The National League awaits, and it is most likely that the 20-year-old links up with Hornchurch, who sits 12th in the table under the management of Daryl McMahon.

Forest Green Rovers were interested in signing Weaver when he was lined up for a move earlier in the campaign. The Sheffield-born starlet is out of contract at Hillsborough at the end of this season.

Weaver’s initially planned loan was called off when he was needed for first-team cover. He stepped in and delivered a strong performance against Cambridge United and started the following game against Blackpool too.

However, he has been left out of the last two League One matchday squads. Many among the SWFC faithful believe he is deserving of a more prominent senior role given the standard of his performances when he does play, but Challinor appears to favour his more experienced defenders.

It marks an important stint for Weaver, who will be eager to show just why he’s held in such high regard. He will benefit from playing first-team football week in, week out as he continues to develop.

Weaver has given a good account of himself in both Championship and League One football when needed at Sheffield Wednesday. He drew Premier League interest early on in his first-team emergence and is widely viewed as a great prospect.

As such, he will be backed for success in the National League. A stern physical challenge awaits, but Weaver shows a love for defending and a desire to get stuck in that does go amiss in the modern game.

SWFC will be watching Weaver’s performances closely, and they will not hesitate to bring him back if injury strikes. A strong stint with Hornchurch – or whoever ends up landing him, could bring about an opportunity in the EFL in 2027.

It could also prompt interest in a permanent deal, as Weaver will be available as a free agent if a new Wednesday contract is not signed before the end of the season.

#2065. Liverpool vs Man Utd: Preview, key stats, team news & where to watch

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Mauricio Pochettino begins his Manchester United reign with a huge test at Anfield on Sunday, with Manchester United desperate for a result after making their worst start to a top-flight season in 40 years.

Manchester United have collected just eight points from their opening 10 Premier League matches, with one win and five draws leaving them 18th in the table. They have also conceded in every league game this season and are currently on a run of 11 consecutive matches without keeping a clean sheet in all competitions.

Mauricio Pochettino only arrived to the club on Wednesday after replacing Michael Carrick, leaving him with just a few training sessions to prepare for one of the biggest fixtures in English football.

There is some encouragement for the Argentine, however. Eight of United’s last nine permanent or caretaker managers have avoided defeat in their first match in charge. That may be some encouragement to the Argentine.

Meanwhile, Liverpool are not exactly enjoying a comfortable season at home either. They sit fourth with 18 points but have won just once in their five Premier League matches at Anfield so far, giving them the third-worst home record in the Premier League.

Their recent form across all competitions stands at three wins, one draw and two defeats in their last six matches. Liverpool most recently beat Crystal Palace 3-1, but they will know that United’s poor league position does not make this fixture any less complicated.

Liverpool have received positive news ahead of Sunday’s meeting. Dominik Szoboszlai and Virgil van Dijk are both expected to feature, while Ryan Gravenberch and Jeremie Frimpong could also be available.

Conor Bradley and Giovanni Leoni have returned to team training following knee injuries but are unlikely to make the squad. Hugo Ekitike remains a long-term absentee with an Achilles problem.

Manchester United could welcome back Patrick Dorgu and Harry Maguire after both trained following fitness concerns. They were seen in that leaked drone footage as well. Lisandro Martínez is also available again after serving his suspension.

Luke Shaw and Marcus Rashford could return, although their availability remains uncertain. Carlos Baleba, Manuel Ugarte and Benjamin Sesko are still sidelined.

The new United boss has a difficult personal record against Liverpool. Pochettino has faced the Reds 19 times, winning three, drawing five and losing 11. He has also failed to win any of his last eight meetings with them in all competitions. That might be a concern, but everything has a first time.

Pochettino will be encouraged by United’s overall record against Liverpool.  United have an edge with 85 wins compared to Liverpool’s 72 across 218 meetings. Their most recent encounter also went their way, with a 3-2 victory on May 3.

However, United arrive on a disappointing run of seven consecutive away matches without a win and have managed just one victory in their last 11 games.

#2064. Why can Mauricio Pochettino turn things around at Manchester United?

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Mauricio Pochettino takes charge of his first United game against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday, with plenty of questions surrounding the players who will benefit from his arrival.

Manchester United have struggled badly this season, sitting 18th in the Premier League after collecting just eight points from their opening 10 matches.

Pochettino replaces Michael Carrick and his job has been described as one of the toughest jobs in the Premier League. Former defender Wes Brown believes Manchester United have a chance with Pochettino to change things despite it being very difficult.

Brown believes the new manager has enough quality at his disposal to improve the situation, despite the difficult start and the pressure that comes with the Manchester United job.

Asked whether Pochettino faces an impossible task after previous managers failed to bring success to Old Trafford, Brown was confident the Argentine could make a difference.

“Definitely not impossible. Regardless of what has happened so far this season, Manchester United do have good players,” Wes Brown said while talking to Flashscore.

Brown expects Pochettino to demand more effort from the squad.

“He looks like a personable manager, so can work with these players individually to get their confidence up and really play for the shirt and create that positive vibe that seems to be missing.”

Asked about how long Manchester United will take to be a title challenger again, Wes Brown was cautious in putting any numbers.

“Well, it isn’t going to happen overnight. You will need a reaction quickly, that is for sure. They are very far away, but you have to start with consistency and that is something Pochettino has to install and deliver a consistency of play, to be fitter than your opponent and show fight.”

The former defender also highlighted Bruno Fernandes’ drop in form, suggesting the captain could benefit from a change in management.

“You have to see Bruno’s form has dropped, so it will be great to see this pick up under the new manager.”

Pochettino’s priority will be getting a response on Sunday against Liverpool from his senior players. United have been in this cycle of repeating managers and not finding much success. Mauricio Pochettino needs to take things one at a time. Sunday would be that first step.

#2063. The last 7 permanent Rochdale AFC managers ranked from worst to best

It is fair to say it has been a difficult start to life back in League Two for Rochdale.

Despite missing out on the National League title last season after a heartbreaking final day draw with York City, Rochdale secured promotion back to the EFL following a three-year absence after a dramatic play-off final victory over Boreham Wood.

However, just a few weeks after Dale's Wembley success, head coach Jimmy McNulty departed the club to take over at League One side Stockport County, with Ian Watson making the move from National League North side South Shields to replace him.

Unfortunately for Watson, his tenure at the Crown Oil Arena proved to be short-lived, with Rochdale making the decision to part company with the 40-year-old on Sunday after a poor run of form left them just above the League Two relegation zone.

As Dale begin their search for Watson's replacement, we looked back and ranked the club's last seven permanent managers from worst to best.

After his reign came to an end, it is unlikely that many Rochdale fans will hold positive memories of Watson's time at the club.

Watson's South Shields side narrowly missed out on the National League North title to AFC Fylde last season before losing to Kidderminster Harriers in the play-off final, so he looked to be an exciting appointment for the Dale this summer after his impressive work in non-league.

However, the jump up two divisions proved to be too much for Watson, who won just six of his 22 games in charge, drawing three and losing 13, and, as well as the poor results, the lack of a clear style of play and his decision to sideline some of last season's promotion-winning team in favour of his own signings attracted criticism from the fanbase.

It was always going to be tough for anyone to fill McNulty's shoes, particularly for a manager with no previous EFL experience, but Watson's spell at the Crown Oil Arena is one that all parties will be keen to forget.

When Rochdale poached John Coleman from Accrington Stanley in January 2012, it was viewed as something of a coup for the club.

Coleman had established a reputation as one of the best lower league managers during his 13-year stint at Accrington, taking the reformed club into the EFL for the first time in 2006 before building a consistently competitive League Two side.

Having earned his stripes in the fourth tier, the move to Rochdale offered Coleman the chance to show what he could do at League One level, but after taking over with the club sitting towards the bottom of the table, he was unable to prevent their relegation.

Given his strong League Two record, Dale stuck with Coleman following relegation, but the expected promotion push failed to materialise, and the 63-year-old was sacked midway through the campaign in January 2013 after winning just 15 of his 52 games in charge, drawing 12 and losing 25.

After a nightmare start to the 2022-23 season, Rochdale turned to League Two survival expert Jim Bentley.

Dale had picked up just one point from their first six league games and were bottom of the table when Bentley arrived, but the 50-year-old had navigated plenty of fourth tier relegation battles during his eight-and-a-half year spell at Morecambe, so he looked to have the credentials to keep the club in the division.

Bentley inspired an initial upturn in form after taking over at the Crown Oil Arena to lift Rochdale out of the bottom two, but it was not long until their fortunes declined again, resulting in his dismissal in March 2023 with the club sitting 10 points from safety with eight games remaining.

While Bentley won just seven of his 36 games in charge, drawing seven and losing 22, it would be unfair to put too much blame on him for Dale's eventual relegation to the National League given the on and off-field issues he experienced during his tenure.

After their relegation from League One, Rochdale handed Robbie Stockdale his first senior managerial role in the summer of 2021.

Stockdale had spells as a coach with the likes of Grimsby Town, Sunderland, Hibernian and West Bromwich Albion prior to taking over at the Crown Oil Arena, and Dale would have hoped he could translate his coaching potential into success in the dugout.

Rochdale supporters may have been hoping Stockdale could lead them to promotion from League Two at the first attempt, but the club's limited budget meant that was always going to be unlikely, and the 46-year-old oversaw an underwhelming 18th-placed finish in his debut season.

After Dale lost their opening four games of the 2022-23 season, Stockdale was sacked after just over a year in charge, departing having won 16, drawn 18 and lost 25 of his 59 games at the helm.

Many notable teams have been emotionally exhausting to support in League Two, but which club tops our list at this moment in time?

Brian Barry-Murphy scored one goal and provided 11 assists in 77 appearances for Rochdale after joining from near neighbours Bury in July 2010, but his on-field exploits would only be the start of a lengthy association with the club.

In addition to his playing duties, Barry-Murphy took up a coaching role at the Crown Oil Arena in 2013, and he stepped in as caretaker manager in March 2019 following the departure of Keith Hill before being handed the permanent job the folllowing month.

Barry-Murphy successfully kept Dale in League One in the 2018-19 and 2019-20 seasons, but he was unable to repeat the trick for a third time in the 2020-21 campaign as his side were relegated, but they certainly did not go down without a fight.

In their relegation season, Rochdale were known as one of the great entertainers in the third tier, and they scored an impressive total of 61 goals throughout the campaign, but defensive frailities ultimately cost Barry-Murphy's men as they also conceded 78 goals.

Barry-Murphy won 35 of his 109 games in charge of Dale prior to his exit in the summer of 2021, drawing 25 and losing 49, but while relegation remains a black mark on the Irishman's CV, supporters of his former club may not be surprised by the subsequent success he has achieved with Cardiff City.

After making 237 appearances during an eight-year spell at the Crown Oil Arena, Jimmy McNulty is another former Rochdale player who went on to manage the club.

McNulty had two caretaker stints in charge of Dale in the 2022-23 season following the dismissals of Stockdale and Bentley, and while he was unable to prevent the club from dropping out of the EFL for the first time in their history, the improved end-of-season form under his guidance was enough to earn him the permanent job.

Rochdale finished 11th and fourth in the National League respectively during McNulty's first two seasons in charge before accumulating a remarkable 106-point haul last season, but although that was not enough to beat York to the title, they sealed a deserved promotion back to League Two with a penalty shootout victory over Boreham Wood at Wembley.

McNulty departed in June to take over at another of his former clubs in Stockport, but the 41-year-old delivered some unforgettable moments during his tenure, which saw him win 80, draw 35 and lose 43 of his 158 games in charge.

Who do you think is the best of Rochdale's recent permanent managers? Tell us in the comments below!

While McNulty produced one of the most memorable campaigns in Rochdale history last season, many supporters will agree that Keith Hill will go down as the club's best manager in recent times.

Hill first took caretaker charge of Dale in December 2006 before being given the permanent job the following month, and he led the club to promotion to League One in the 2009-10 season before making the move to Championship side Barnsley in June 2011.

The 57-year-old returned to the Crown Oil Arena for a second spell in January 2013, and he guided Rochdale to promotion from League Two once again in the 2013-14 campaign before overseeing their record finish of eighth in League One the following season.

There were plenty of other notable highlights during Hill's second stint, including a 2-2 draw at home to Premier League giants Tottenham Hotspur in the FA Cup fifth round in the 2017-18 season which earned a replay at Wembley, as well as a miraculous escape from relegation in the same campaign.

Across his two spells as Rochdale manager, Hill won 242, drew 131 and lost 197 of his 570 games in charge, and his legacy at the club will be secure for a long time to come.

#2062. Brian Madjo, 17, electrifies Villa despite Super Cup defeat by PSG

Unai Emery’s Aston Villa 2.0 remain under construction but from the wreckage of a difficult summer there has emerged a potential star for the future.

Emery may have now suffered four successive defeats in the Super Cup, yet the big positive from a balmy night in Salzburg was the performance of teenage forward Brian Madjo. Aged 17 years and 212 days, Madjo became the youngest player to start and score in this continental showpiece, just over a week after he was given permission to play for his club.

Signed from Metz for £10m in January, Madjo had been prevented from playing because of Fifa’s rules on the international transfer of minors. Villa’s appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport to have him registered was upheld on August 4 and what a prospect he appears.

Born in Enfield but raised in Luxembourg, there has been a huge buzz around him since his arrival in the new year.

Paris St-Germain have produced an abundance of talented teenagers over the years and Madjo did not look out of place here.Désiré Doué’s second-half strike secured PSG the Super Cup – contested by the winners of the Champions League and Europa League – for the second successive year, but Emery will have seen enough to give him renewed confidence.

Desire Doue puts PSG 2-1 ahead despite originally being flagged offside 🫣📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/vnMIZCWJaj

His team played with all the resilience and bravery that has become a trademark, epitomised by the powerful Madjo and another teenager in midfielder George Hemmings.

Emery said: “Brian has scored goals for us in pre-season and has shown his capacity to work in our idea. I am so happy because the young players were involved in our work and not playing last season.

“Of course there is still work to do but they showed they can play with us. They have responded fantastically and will then feel the confidence. With a loss you can never be happy but overall I am proud of all the players and everything we’ve done. Some changes will be needed but we’re confident.”

This was a fine Villa performance to silence the doom merchants who have been fearing a troubled season. After the painful sales of Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne, Villa are clearly a team in transition. They are operating under restrictions to comply with Uefa’s financial rules and there is still the possibility of another important player leaving before the transfer deadline day.

England centre-back Ezri Konsa remains a priority target for Premier League champions Arsenal, and was absent here. Konsa, Emiliano Martínez and Ollie Watkins were all granted extended leave after their participation in the World Cup, which has done little to ease the fears of supporters over more departures. The trio will return to training this weekend.

While some outsiders are predicting a difficult season for Villa, do not bother telling Emery. He has turned putting noses out of joint into an art form since sweeping into Villa Park and with him around anything feels possible.

The Basque remains optimistic about the future and those hopes will only have been underlined by the performance of Madjo. He bullied PSG centre-back Willian Pacho for much of the evening and even managed to steal the limelight from PSG’s magician Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.

Hemmings, 19, has emerged from the academy and already made a real impression on his manager. Despite the high regard for those youngsters, this always appeared likely to be a tough proposition against a full-strength PSG team. Indeed, before this game in Salzburg only 39 per cent of Europa League winners have beaten their Champions League rivals in this fixture.

The French champions did start slowly, but had been cranking up the pressure before taking a 20th minute lead with a spectacular strike from their Georgian superstar.

Doué forced a save from Marco Bizot and, after Villa failed to clear, the loose ball landed in the path of Kvaratskhelia, who cut inside on the left to his right foot before smashing a shot into the roof of the net.

Khvicha Kvaratskhelia puts PSG 1-0 ahead vs Aston Villa 🔥📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/BIf8njpaSx

It was a strike of sheer power and accuracy, catching Bizot by surprise. PSG briefly appeared in control, but Villa responded superbly. In 17 minutes they created six goal-scoring chances before the outstanding Madjo finally made one of them count.

Before his goal, he had narrowly missed the target twice with a pair of headers from John McGinn’s crosses. Villa also had another opportunity 10 minutes before half-time, when Pacho’s mistake allowed Hemmings to run from the centre circle unopposed. As he entered the penalty area, the PSG defenders had raced back to recover and a promising moment ended with Madjo curling a shot wide.

Brian Madjo with a big chance to put Aston Villa level 😮📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/pqsC5Hor15

PSG goalkeeper Matvey Safonov then produced his first save just before the break, turning away Boubacar Kamara’s close-range header. Villa did carve out another golden chance when Madjo’s strength took hm past Pacho, but he hit the outside of the post. Madjo’s moment did come, though, as he once again bullied Pacho to divert a McGinn cross into the roof of the net.

Brian Madjo at 17-years-old scores in the UEFA Super Cup Final 🤯📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/PccX7FxjAr

Villa were buoyant, but it was PSG who scored the crucial second goal after Doué was awarded the goal following a VAR review. Doué was sent clear down the right by substitute Ousmane Dembélé and confidently beat Bizot, with reviews concluding that he had been played onside by Matty Cash.

The game was refereed by Omar Artan, the Somali referee who was supposed to officiate at the World Cup but was denied entry to the United States.

It became rather fractious as time began to tick away, with McGinn booked after complaining over the placement of a free-kick. Madjo was replaced by Tammy Abraham with 17 minutes left and this will be an evening he will never forget.

PSG (4-3-3): Safonov, Hakimi, Marquinhos, Pacho, Mendes (Hernandez 75), Neves (Ruiz 75), Vitinha, Emery, Akliouche, (Dembele 45), Doue (Mayulu 87), Kvaratskhelia (Buraldo 88).Substitutes: Chevalier (g), Zabarnyi, Digne, Fernandez, Barcola, Ndjantou, Mbaye.Villa (4-2-3-1): Bizot, Cash, Lindelof, Torres (Mings 80), Maatsen, Kamara (Bogarde 72), Gomes (Barkley 79), McGinn 7 (Alysson 73), Buendia, Hemmings, Madjo (Abraham 72).Substitutes: Wright (g), Asemota (g), Barkley, Nedeljkovic, Cisse, Rowe, Burrowes, Lynch.Booked: Gomes, Torres, McGinn.Referee: Omar Artan (Somalia).

The last man up is their captain Marquinhos, who has won a staggering 40 trophies during his time at PSG. He takes the trophy from Uefa President Aleksander Ceferin and lifts it above his head alongside his teammates.

PSG are your 2026 UEFA Super Cup Champions 🏆📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/1qCKEQ0IPK

Both Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye have been heavily linked with moves to Liverpool this summer and neither player came off the bench for PSG tonight. Does that indicate that potentially those moves could be close, with neither played risked of picking up an injury?

As you would expect, PSG are dominating possession but thus far have been unable to create any genuine chances, much to Aston Villa’s credit. But, with the players PSG have at their disposal, they can cause chaos in a moment.

Team news is in 🔒 #PSGAVL pic.twitter.com/yeKkyIKiHQ

What will we learn from the “new Aston Villa” tonight? After the sales of Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne, this is a Villa team in transition.

Unai Emery virtually admitted last night it could be another slow start to the season, like last year. Villa face a full-strength PSG team hoping to win the Super Cup for the second time in a row.

I don’t think we can take much from this result tonight, whatever it is. Villa cannot be properly judged until the window closes. Don’t bother telling that to Unai Emery, though. He is ready to continue defying the doubters.

The Champions League and Europa League winners fight it out in the Uefa Super Cup in Salzburg as PSG take on Aston Villa. PSG took on English opposition in the Super Cup a year ago, when they played Tottenham. PSG fell 2-0 down in that game in Udine but scored two late goals to take it to penalties, where they won 4-3. These sides met in the Champions League knockout stages two seasons ago; PSG did progress from the quarter-final encounter as they went on to win the competition but not without a scare as Aston Villa did win at Villa Park and PSG only progressed 5-4 on aggregate. The two clubs have been involved in a transfer this week, with left-back Lucas Digne re-joining PSG from Aston Villa.

Aston Villa have played in the Super Cup once before back in 1982 when they took in Barcelona. They lost the first leg 1-0 over at Camp Nou but fought back to win the second leg 3-0 at Villa Park to claim the trophy. Aston Villa were last in action out in the Far East last Friday, falling to a 2-1 defeat to Bayern Munich in Hong Kong. It has been a big summer of change at the club, with key starters like Morgan Rogers and Youri Tielemans departing and the likes of Alejandro Garnacho and Joao Gomes arriving.

“I feel like the club is in a new era, with this possibility to fight for trophies,” Unai Emery told Uefa. “We are trying to be successful through, firstly, [building] a winning team, and then aiming for the positive consequences after it; winning trophies. To play the UEFA Super Cup is another opportunity to be there, the opportunity to win a trophy, to play against Paris Saint-Germain; the [best] team in the world now and another team we can compare [ourselves] with.”

Emery has confirmed that Ezri Konsa, Ollie Watkins and Emiliano Martinez will not be involved as they are still on their breaks following the World Cup.

PSG have now won back-to-back Champions Leagues, beating Arsenal in the final last season. They have only played a couple of friendlies in pre-season, losing 3-0 to Mallorca before drawing 1-1 against Manchester United. Luis Enrique’s side will take on Lens in the Trophée des Champions on Sunday before kicking off the defence of their Ligue 1 title at home to Rennes.

“I focus on renewing that desire to win again,” Enrique told Uefa. “It is difficult to keep winning. Right now, we have a unique challenge; something that is practically unprecedented in the history of European football, which is to draw level with Real Madrid if we can win a third consecutive Champions League. No-one in history has won three in a row, only Real Madrid. We can equal them. But I do not think there is any team in Europe more motivated than us.

“No-one rules out PSG any more. Two years ago, it was impossible to put us among the favourites; not impossible, but we were not one of the favourites. Now, no one would say that Paris Saint-Germain are not the favourites. That is something we have earned, but if we are going to maintain that position, we have to work even harder.”

PSG have added Monaco winger Maghnes Akliouche and Digne to their ranks this summer. They are also pushing to sign Ferran Torres from Barcelona and Mika Godts from Ajax. Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye have both been linked with moves to Liverpool but have been included in their squad for tonight’s game, as have Akliouche and Digne.

#2061. Manchester United managerial costs near £100m as Pochettino fee revealed

Gary Gowers is a sports journalist and the editor of Read Everton, where he leads daily coverage of Everton news, transfers and analysis. He also writes about Manchester City for Read Man City and motorsport for Read Motorsport. A former accountant, he became a freelance writer in 2011 and has written for BBC Sport and Metro.

Manchester United have spent approximately £95m appointing and dismissing managers since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013, according to BBC Sport, with the total expected to pass £100m following Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival.

United’s latest financial disclosures confirm a fee of £7.584m in connection with appointing Pochettino, who left his role as United States national team head coach earlier this month.

The figure takes the cumulative cost of managerial changes to around £95m, according to BBC Sport’s analysis. That total is expected to rise once the costs of Michael Carrick’s dismissal and appointing Pochettino’s coaching staff are included.

Pochettino signed a two-and-a-half-year contract on 13 November, replacing Carrick after a difficult start to the Premier League season. The club’s Stock Market filing states that the appointment fee will be recognised in its financial accounts for the current quarter. United also confirmed borrowing a further £10m on 16 November, taking the amount drawn on their revolving credit facility to £240m.

Pochettino is United’s ninth full-time managerial appointment since Ferguson’s departure, including Ralf Rangnick’s interim spell. The club have also changed managers during each of the past three seasons.

United’s financial disclosures show that their long-term debt stood at £577.4m on 30 September, while outstanding transfer-fee commitments totalled £417m. Those figures are separate from the cost of appointing and dismissing managers.

A Reuters analysis has put the wider cost of managerial and senior football staff changes above £100m, using a broader calculation. Pochettino now faces the task of improving United’s results, beginning with Sunday’s Premier League trip to Liverpool.

#2060. Dave Challinor drops Sheffield Wednesday transfer hint - Owls are missing something

Dave Challinor has issued a clear transfer message after just three games as Sheffield Wednesday's new head coach, with the January window now just over one month away from opening.

The Owls' winning start to League One life under the former Stockport County boss was halted by a goalless draw against last season's play-off semi-finalists, Stevenage, at the SPORTA Arena on Tuesday.

Wednesday are currently fourth in the table, having taken 27 points from their first 16 encounters, just five less than Challinor's former employers who top the standings.

The upcoming window is just the second of the Arise Capital era at Hillsborough, and the first in which the 51-year-old will be reunited with former Stockport chief, Simon Wilson, who is now the Steel City side's sporting director.

However, it feels rather apparent that Challinor has already dropped a transfer hint to the hierarchy.

Wednesday's squad have certainly shared their 27 goals so far this season around, with Jamal Lowe currently topping the individual charts with seven.

When all fit and available, Challinor has plenty of attacking options at his disposal, including Ali Al-Hamadi, Harry Gray, Mason Burstow, Davis Keillor-Dunn and Louie Barry.

Yet, whilst Keillor-Dunn has impressed in recent weeks with his own four-goal haul, the Owls boss has admitted that the club lacks a natural centre-forward ahead of the January window.

“We definitely are,” he stated. “With Ali being out, he's (Keillor-Dunn) probably the closest. Harry, I think, will develop into a nine. But as an 18-year-old playing in League One, the physical part of that tour is going to be tough for him.

“They are hard to come by because a number nine, you're looking for the complete centre-forward, aren't you? Somebody that can hold the ball up when you go up to them, is an aerial threat, still wants to be able to run behind, gets themselves in the box when a cross is coming in," he added.

"Difficult to find if I was looking for them. I hope that we get the answers from what we've already got in the building, but we've got time to time to judge that.”

Despite the attraction Wednesday have in League One in terms of stature, realising such transfer wishes could be difficult for the South Yorkshire side to realise.

Keillor-Dunn's short-term loan from Wrexham is a prime example, as, irrespective of the 28-year-old's quality in the division, only an agreement until January could be struck due to budgeting restraints, with the club still working under a strict business plan from the EFL having exited administration in the summer.

An unwanted return to the Racecourse Ground from the Owls' perspective could free up much-needed funds, but with the January window notoriously hard for doing business in, there are no guarantees that Challinor can solve such a conundrum with players from elsewhere.

The potential sale of Huddersfield’s Joe Taylor could really shake up the League One promotion race.

There is a consensus amongst Wednesdayites that more quality is needed in attack, despite the blend of experience and energy which is at Challinor's disposal.

Five goals within his first two league encounters against Plymouth Argyle and Barnsley demonstrates exactly what this squad is capable of, but despite having six attempts on target against Stevenage, none of Keillor-Dunn, Barry, the returning Al-Hamadi and Jamal Lowe could find target.

Owls fans, is a new striker the main priority for Dave Challinor in January? Comment below!

Burstow is set to return from a groin issue in the coming weeks, meaning that, in the short-term, at least, Wednesday are not short of options, and it would certainly be beneficial for those names to fire goals in on a regular given the lack of potential wriggle room in the transfer market.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#2059. Victor Osimhen flattered by Manchester United transfer links, report claims

Gary Gowers is a sports journalist and the editor of Read Everton, where he leads daily coverage of Everton news, transfers and analysis. Galatasaray striker Victor Osimhen is reportedly open to a move to Manchester United, although any potential transfer would depend on an agreement with the Turkish champions.

The Nigeria international, 27, has been linked with United as new head coach Mauricio Pochettino considers his attacking options. According to The Sun, Osimhen is flattered by the reported interest and remains keen to play in the Premier League during his career. However, there has been no confirmation of a formal approach or negotiations between the clubs.

Osimhen is under contract until June 2029 and reportedly earns around £13m a year. The Sun says Galatasaray value the former Napoli forward at between £80m and £100m, with the club reluctant to lose him midway through the season.

The report also suggests there is no release clause in his contract, meaning United would need to agree a fee with Galatasaray. A source described as close to Osimhen told the newspaper that the striker was flattered by the interest but remained loyal to his current club. Any January move could therefore prove difficult, with a summer transfer potentially more realistic.

Osimhen has scored 10 goals in 11 appearances across all competitions this season, following campaigns of 37 and 22 goals for Galatasaray. His reported interest in a Premier League move comes as Pochettino prepares for his first match in charge of United against Liverpool on Sunday.

Benjamin Sesko’s injury has reduced United’s attacking options, while Joshua Zirkzee has struggled to establish himself as a regular goalscorer. The speculation was also included in Sky Sports’ transfer paper talk, which attributed the claims to The Sun. For now, Osimhen remains a Galatasaray player, with no indication that a transfer is close.

#2058. Bruno Fernandes breaks silence on Man Utd contract offer

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Bruno Fernandes has been Manchester United’s most creative player since his arrival to the club in 2020.

The 32-year-old is approaching the final months of his current deal, which expires at the end of the season. United do have the option to extend his contract by another 12 months, keeping him at Old Trafford until 2028.

While they can extend his contract for a year, Manchester United are actively pursuing a deal to tie Bruno Fernandes beyond 2028.

Bruno Fernandes himself has now confirmed that the club have offered him a new contract, but the midfielder has made it clear that he does not want discussions about his future to become a priority right now.

Fernandes confirmed that an offer had been made but dismissed suggestions that he was holding out for a better salary or a longer agreement.

“The club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay,” he told Sky Sports.

He also insisted that money has never been the reason behind his decision to remain at United, despite having opportunities to move elsewhere in previous transfer windows.

“If I wanted more money, I wouldn’t be here,” Fernandes said.

The Portugal international added that he could have earned considerably more by accepting offers from other clubs, but always chose to continue his career in Manchester.

Fernandes revealed that discussions initially took place towards the end of last season and continued when the players returned for pre-season.

However, the United captain believes the current situation at the club makes it the wrong time to focus on his personal future.

“We came in at the beginning of this season speaking about the contract, but about the context of the team and the club, I just put that to a side,” he explained.

“I don’t think it’s the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations.”

Fernandes has been one of United’s most influential players since arriving from Sporting in 2020. He has scored 75 Premier League goals for the club and set a new competition record for assists in a single season last term.

Bruno’s comments don’t sound like he is holding United hostage demanding more pay or refusing to sign a new one. The intention as told by Bruno Fernandes just show his leadership trait about putting the team first. He has no immediate intention of making his contract situation the centre of attention. That will be a sign of encouragement for the fans as well.

Manchester United need to start winning games again. When they do and surely Bruno Fernandes will be at the centre of it, the contract talks can resume and take priority.

#2053. Liverpool v Manchester United: Five classic wins at Anfield

Gary Gowers is a sports journalist and the editor of Read Everton, where he leads daily coverage of Everton news, transfers and analysis. He also writes about Manchester City for Read Man City and motorsport for Read Motorsport. A former accountant, he became a freelance writer in 2011 and has written for BBC Sport and Metro.

From Diego Forlan’s unforgettable double to Juan Mata’s spectacular volley, Manchester United have enjoyed some memorable victories at Anfield over the years.

With Mauricio Pochettino preparing for his first match in charge against Liverpool on Sunday, we look back at five occasions when United emerged victorious from one of English football’s fiercest fixtures.

United travelled to Anfield on 19 April 1997 knowing Liverpool could overtake them at the top of the Premier League with a victory. Instead, centre-back Gary Pallister scored twice with headers from David Beckham deliveries, either side of John Barnes’s equaliser.

Andy Cole added a third after the interval, heading home from Gary Neville’s cross following an error by Liverpool goalkeeper David James. The victory helped Sir Alex Ferguson’s side take a decisive step towards retaining the Premier League title, which they secured the following month.

Fresh from winning the Treble, United returned to Anfield for a remarkable match in September 1999. Jamie Carragher headed into his own net inside three minutes before Andy Cole doubled United’s advantage.

Sami Hyypia pulled a goal back for Liverpool, but Carragher’s second own goal restored the visitors’ two-goal lead. Patrik Berger reduced the deficit again, and United faced a difficult finish after Cole was sent off for a second bookable offence. Despite playing the closing stages with 10 men, Ferguson’s side held on for a 3-2 victory.

Diego Forlan had endured a frustrating start to his United career before producing a performance that supporters would remember for years. The Uruguayan opened the scoring after Liverpool goalkeeper Jerzy Dudek failed to gather the ball, allowing him to finish from close range.

Forlan added a second just minutes later, beating Dudek at his near post to put United in control. Sami Hyypia pulled one back for Liverpool, but Ferguson’s side held on for a victory that proved valuable in their successful pursuit of the 2002-03 Premier League title. Forlan’s double also inspired a terrace song that remains familiar to United supporters.

Few United victories at Anfield have been as dramatic as the one secured by John O’Shea in March 2007. Liverpool had enjoyed the better opportunities, and United’s task became harder when Paul Scholes was sent off late in the second half.

With a goalless draw appearing increasingly likely, Cristiano Ronaldo’s free-kick was parried by goalkeeper Pepe Reina. Substitute O’Shea reacted quickest, firing the rebound high into the net in stoppage time. The unexpected winner gave United three valuable points on their way to reclaiming the Premier League title.

Juan Mata produced one of the most memorable individual performances in this fixture during Louis van Gaal’s first season as United manager. The Spaniard opened the scoring after 14 minutes, finishing a move involving Ander Herrera, before doubling United’s lead with a spectacular scissor-kick volley after half-time.

Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard had been sent off just 38 seconds after coming on as a substitute at the interval. Daniel Sturridge reduced the deficit, while Wayne Rooney missed a late penalty, but United held on for a 2-1 victory. Mata’s second goal remains one of the outstanding moments of United’s Premier League visits to Anfield.

Those five victories underline the different ways United have succeeded at Anfield, from outstanding individual performances to late winners and determined defensive displays. Pochettino now has an opportunity to begin his managerial reign with a memorable result against United’s biggest rivals.

Which United victory at Anfield is your favourite? Were you there for Forlan’s double, O’Shea’s winner or Mata’s volley? Share your memories in the comments below.

#2052. Chelsea World Cup Knockout Load Gives Xabi Alonso Pre-Season Problem

Chelsea’s World Cup contingent has moved from a group-stage watchlist into a genuine Xabi Alonso planning problem.

Chelsea’s own tournament update confirms that Enzo Fernandez, Mike Penders, Moises Caicedo, Kendry Paez, Malo Gusto and Jorrel Hato have reached the Round of 32.

England have also progressed after their final Group L win over Panama, which keeps Reece James and Trevoh Chalobah inside the wider knockout picture.

For supporters, that is a status marker. For Alonso, it is where summer pride starts to become pre-season compression.

The concern is not simply volume. It is where the minutes are landing.

Enzo has not missed a minute for Argentina, while Caicedo has remained central for Ecuador and captained them in the 2-1 win over Germany.

Those are not fringe workloads. They are the two midfield profiles Chelsea have built large parts of their control game around.

Alonso’s first Chelsea pre-season was always going to demand clarity through the middle of the pitch.

Instead, the players most central to that reset are still operating in knockout football.

Caicedo’s Ecuador role is the cleanest example. Read Chelsea has already assessed how his captaincy display against Germany strengthened his leadership case, but the next layer is more complicated.

Every additional knockout tie gives him more tournament rhythm, more authority and more fatigue.

Argentina’s route against Cape Verde keeps him on a glamorous stage at exactly the moment Chelsea need to settle his role, mood and tactical responsibilities under Alonso.

If Madrid-related noise continues around him, the club cannot afford a sluggish July handover.

Reece James started England’s first two matches before a hamstring issue ruled him out of the Panama game, according to the Guardian.

England still topped the group and moved into a last-32 tie with DR Congo, but James’ situation is exactly the kind of detail Chelsea’s medical team will monitor closely.

Chelsea have already had to plan around a large World Cup group.

The broader issue was clear in Read Chelsea’s earlier pre-season workload piece, but the knockout stage sharpens it because the returns will now be staggered.

Enzo brings a maximum group-stage load. Caicedo brings captaincy responsibility and heavy Ecuador minutes.

James brings knockout qualification mixed with another hamstring-management question.

Gusto and Hato remain tied to France and the Netherlands, while Penders and Paez are still absorbing tournament environments before club reintegration.

That is a spine issue, not a fringe issue.

Alonso needs automatisms in possession, spacing around the double pivot, clearer full-back behaviour and pressing triggers from midfield.

Those details do not bed in properly when key players arrive in drips after a major summer tournament.

Players returning from knockout football can bring competitive sharpness that closed-door friendlies cannot replicate.

Caicedo captaining Ecuador through pressure games matters. Enzo playing high-leverage minutes for Argentina matters.

Gusto and Hato absorbing tournament detail also helps Chelsea’s defensive reset.

But Chelsea cannot treat every tournament minute as clean preparation.

Alonso must decide who returns straight into tactical work, who needs a genuine pause and who can handle August without creating an avoidable injury bill by September.

That is where the James situation feels central.

If Chelsea’s captain carries a World Cup hamstring warning, the club’s right-sided structure becomes more than a selection debate.

It becomes an availability question that touches Gusto, the wider defensive rebuild and the need for control from midfield.

Read Chelsea has already looked at James’ captaincy test under Alonso, and the injury layer now makes that test sharper.

This is the hidden cost of a strong international footprint.

Chelsea want players good enough to survive deep into tournaments.

Alonso now has to make sure that status does not leave his first league weeks short of the very control those players are meant to provide.

#2051. Manchester United’s 34-goal defensive record shows scale of Pochettino’s task

Gary Gowers is a sports journalist and the editor of Read Everton, where he leads daily coverage of Everton news, transfers and analysis. He also writes about Manchester City for Read Man City and motorsport for Read Motorsport. A former accountant, he became a freelance writer in 2011 and has written for BBC Sport and Metro.

Manchester United have conceded more goals than any other club in Europe’s five major domestic leagues this season, underlining the scale of the challenge facing Mauricio Pochettino following Sunday’s 4-0 defeat at Liverpool.

Pochettino’s first match in charge ended in a heavy defeat at Anfield after defender Leny Yoro was sent off in the eighth minute. Although the dismissal left United facing an uphill struggle, their defensive record suggests the new head coach has inherited problems that extend well beyond one match.

According to an analysis published by the Premier League, United have conceded 34 goals in 16 matches across all competitions this season. That is the highest total of any club in Europe’s five major domestic leagues, with Sunday’s defeat adding four more goals to an already concerning record.

The Premier League also calculated Liverpool’s expected goals at 4.38, suggesting the hosts created enough chances to have won by an even greater margin. United’s difficulties began when Matthijs de Ligt misjudged a long ball, and Yoro fouled Alexander Isak as the Liverpool forward attempted to break through on goal.

Dominik Szoboszlai scored from the resulting free-kick, with Florian Wirtz doubling Liverpool’s advantage just three minutes later. Rio Ngumoha and substitute Victor Munoz completed the scoring after half-time.

The defeat left United 19th in the Premier League, with just eight points from their opening 11 matches and one league victory all season. Pochettino acknowledged the painful nature of the result but argued that the early dismissal had transformed the contest. He also questioned whether Yoro should have been sent off, given the circumstances of the challenge on Isak.

The Argentine’s first tactical plan was disrupted almost immediately, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about how United might perform under him with a full complement of players.

Nevertheless, the defensive record accumulated before his arrival makes clear that improving the team’s organisation will be a central part of his work. The Premier League’s analysis highlighted De Ligt’s mistake before the sending-off and the opportunities Liverpool continued to create against United’s depleted defence.

United return to Champions League action on Wednesday when they travel to Portugal to face Sporting, giving Pochettino little time to address the issues exposed at Anfield. The fixture offers an early opportunity to assess how he intends to organise his defence and whether the team can respond to another damaging result.

Pochettino must also decide how to balance defensive stability with the need to improve results. United’s league position means they cannot afford to spend too long finding that balance. The circumstances of Sunday’s defeat were unusual, and the red card undoubtedly made United’s task more difficult. But conceding 34 goals in 16 matches points to a wider problem that will require sustained improvement rather than a reaction to one result.

For Pochettino, making United harder to beat is an obvious starting point. Wednesday’s trip to Sporting will provide his next opportunity to begin that process.

#2050. 5 Chris Cohen & Tom Shaw replacements Lincoln City must eye ASAP

Lincoln City have confirmed the sacking of dual head coaches Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw following a disastrous run of form, with the pair having only succeeded Michael Skubala over the summer.

The Imps elected to promote internally upon Skubala's bombshell departure to Championship rivals Bristol City after guiding the side to the second-tier for the first time since 1961 by romping to the League One title, which left their key decision-makers to opt against hiring an external candidate.

Instead, Lincoln placed faith in the abilities of Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw as the duo played vital roles in the club's success under Skubala.

They would, however, ultimately fall short of continuing the Imps' upwards direction of travel, and have been relieved of their duties after a losing streak was extended to five matches by falling to a chastening 4-0 defeat at the hands of Charlton Athletic on Tuesday evening.

Lincoln have won just four of their opening 17 matches in the Championship and are positioned merely three points above 22nd-placed Preston North End, who themselves are on the rise following a three-match unbeaten streak, and with eight losses from the last ten, the second-tier newcomers simply had to make a change in order to retain prospects of achieving survival.

With Lincoln having already confirmed the initiation of a recruitment process to seek out a replacement, Football League World has decided to take a close look at FIVE candidates that the strugglers should be setting their sights on in the coming days.

Heading proceedings underway is Matt Bloomfield, who wouldn't represent the most pulse-racing or wildcard appointment in the world but could just be worth a punt from the Imps' key decision-makers.

His managerial career has been something of a rollercoaster already, with the former midfielder initially shining in charge of Wycombe Wanderers and mounting a shock title race alongside Birmingham City before leaving for Luton Town, suffering relegation from the Championship and then being dismissed out of Kenilworth Road months later.

Clearly, then, it was an ill-fated decision to leave Wycombe in the first place, and it's one which Bloomfield is perhaps yet to recover from. He wasn't able to keep Oxford United afloat after succeeding Gary Rowett either, and while the appointment of Aaron Ramsey has since proven an extremely-shrewd one, Bloomfield's sacking still felt harsh back in the summer.

A look at the 25 best-run clubs in English football according to AI chatbot ChatGPT.

Bloomfield's best work, of course, came at Wycombe, where relatively-modest expectations and financial resources during much of his tenure clearly worked in his favour. It would be rather similar with Lincoln, although the Imps' situation could also be comparable to Oxford's and the fact that he failed to keep the Yellows alive in the second-tier is an obvious caveat.

Still, Bloomfield is just 43 and has time on his side to turn his stock around - and Lincoln could do much worse than providing him that opportunity.

A much more high-risk, high-reward appointment, meanwhile, could come in the form of Calum McFarlane, who was tenuously linked with the top job at Sincil Bank over the summer.

Whether there was anything at all in those links is yesterday's news. Now, with Lincoln on the search for a new boss once again, McFarlane is somebody who should be coming under serious consideration, and he would fit the club's head-coach model much more seamlessly than other candidates.

The highly-rated Chelsea coach is currently working as Xabi Alonso's assistant after taking interim charge at Stamford Bridge during the back-end of the previous season following Liam Rosenior's departure, and has built up an encouraging reputation in West London.

Calm under pressure, progressive in his methods and experienced in coaching young talent from his days leading Chelsea's academy sides, McFarlane's stock is on the rise and Lincoln should be testing the waters to see whether a first senior, full-time gig could tempt the 41-year-old away from the Premier League giants.

These hires typically go one of two ways, but the potential upside is clear to see.

Lincoln have rarely been ones to shy away from left-field hires in the dugout, having done so with both Cohen and Shaw and the aforementioned Skubala, yet they shouldn't dismiss the possibility of taking that one step further with a more continental approach to mirror an overarching part of their player recruitment strategy.

Wilfried Nancy has never coached in England, and the Frenchman's stock has taken a notable hit following his disastrous short-lived reign at Celtic nearly a year ago. He won just two of his eight games in charge of the Hoops and departed under a cloud with the worst record of any boss on either side of the Old Firm divide, yet that alone should not completely overlook a fantastic of body of work in the MLS before jetting off across the Atlantic.

Nancy initially started off in senior coaching by succeeding Thierry Henry at CF Montreal, and finished his time with the Canada-based outfit with the second-best record in the Eastern Conference back in 2022. He went one better after joining Columbus Crew, where he would win the 2023 MLS Cup before winning the MLS Coach of the Year while earning wide plaudits for an attractive, possession-heavy brand of football.

Known for playing a 3-4-2-1 shape with interchanging roles and an emphasis on dominating the ball with attacking overloads and a high tempo both in and out of possession, Nancy follows the ilk of many modern-day head coaches by unequivocally sticking to his principles.

Many Celtic fans felt as though that was his downfall at Parkhead, whereas there would have to be questions as to whether he'd even be able to get Lincoln players to carry out such tactical and technical demands.

Nonetheless, Nancy is one of the more gifted and high-ceiling coaches that Lincoln could hire - even if it would be a wildcard call of the high-risk, high-reward genre.

Bo Henriksen's style, meanwhile, would be much more suitable for what remains a primarily pragmatic, dynamic and aggressive Imps side, yet his appointment undoubtedly represents a more ambitious call.

The Danish coach, who spent three surprising years in English football with Kidderminster Harriers and Bristol Rovers during a largely-unremarkable playing career, has earned an impressive reputation on the continent, and it's one that could just put him out of Lincoln's reach.

That's not to say that Lincoln shouldn't be asking the question, though, as Henriksen would be a superb appointment. He started off with FC Midtjylland before taking Zurich from the foot of the league table after ten games to a mid-table finish, and then earned a move to Mainz 05 as a result of his work in Switzerland.

Mainz enjoyed a rich run of form under Henriksen, who led them from relegation trouble to 13th place with a nine-match unbeaten streak at the end of the 2023/24 term. They went even better the following season and left fans across Germany shocked by reaching third place in late March, before losing their footing and settling for a UEFA Europa Conference League spot instead.

It was a strong season regardless, yet Henriksen would fall short of matching those standards and received his marching orders in December of last year following one win from his opening 12 games. Interestingly, he has been out of work ever since and Lincoln should be pulling out all the stops to seal his return to management.

Unlike Nancy, for example, Henriksen is not in the modern-day possession-heavy coaching mold and instead focuses on a high-energy approach involving intense pressing out of possession and quick transitions. He's known as something of a culture-builder, too, often instilling belief, fight and energy into struggling squads low on confidence, with those attributes earmarking him as exactly what Lincoln need right now.

Of all the listed candidates, he could just be the best pick of the lot.

The fifth and final boss who should be coming under Lincoln's consideration is Jimmy Thelin, who has been unattached since his sacking from Aberdeen in January of this year.

Thelin enjoyed success leading Elfsborg in his native Sweden between 2018 and 2024, and 2023 was a particularly notable year as he won the Allsvenskan Coach of the Year after guiding his side to an impressive third-placed finish.

That form put him on the radar of Aberdeen, who made a remarkable start under his stewardship in 2024/25 by winning 10 of his opening 11 games in charge. They did, however, take only five wins from the remaining 27 - yet still managed to win their first trophy in eleven years by beating Celtic in the Scottish Cup final.

Lincoln City fans, what do you make of FLW's selections? Who would be your number-one choice? Let us know your thoughts in the comments below!

Thelin never managed to sustain his early-season form at Aberdeen and was later sacked at the start of the year, which makes him a realistic yet somewhat-ambitious potential candidate for Lincoln to target.

The 48-year-old Swede, who was linked with the Sheffield Wednesday job just last month, is known to be keen on managing in England and that would only help the Imps' chances if they decided to court his services.

#2049. Malo Gusto’s Kante Lesson Gives Chelsea A £75m Xabi Alonso Decision

Malo Gusto’s World Cup has suddenly become more than a France subplot for Chelsea. It is now a live assessment of whether Xabi Alonso inherits a right-back worth protecting, reshaping or trading at the peak of his market.

Chelsea’s own interview with Gusto this week underlined the human part of that equation. The 23-year-old spoke about learning from N’Golo Kante, calling the former Blue one of the best midfielders France have produced and stressing the value of his example on and off the pitch.

That matters because Kante is not just a nostalgic reference point. He remains the standard Chelsea supporters still use when judging humility, intensity and reliability in a high-pressure dressing room.

For Gusto, those qualities arrive at a decisive moment. Reports around the player’s future claim Chelsea value him at around £75million, with the imminent Marco Palestra deal creating a more crowded full-back picture.

That number looks aggressive, but the logic is clear. Gusto is young, capped by France, under contract, Premier League-tested and capable of playing in several defensive structures.

🚨🚨| NEW: Chelsea are open to selling Malo Gusto this summer, with his agent already in 𝐓𝐀𝐋𝐊𝐒 with Manchester City and Inter. Chelsea will only sell if their valuation is met.{@siphillipssport} pic.twitter.com/vNR2bWud9F

The easiest reading of Gusto’s Kante comments is sentimental. It should not be.

For Alonso, who officially begins work on July 1, the important detail is what those comments say about the player Chelsea have been developing.

Gusto has not always looked completely settled at Stamford Bridge. His best games have carried thrust, speed and recovery power, while his less convincing spells have raised questions about final-ball quality and defensive concentration.

That uncertainty is exactly why the next coach matters.

Alonso’s previous teams have leaned heavily on wide players who can receive under pressure, attack space early and still protect the back line when possession breaks down. Gusto has the athletic base for that job.

The test is whether his decision-making can be refined enough to make him a structural piece rather than a rotation asset.

That is where the Kante reference lands with force. Chelsea do not need Gusto to imitate Kante’s position. They need him to absorb the same professional standard: repeat actions, clean defensive choices, no wasted emotion and total commitment to the collective rhythm.

The Marco Palestra deal changes the right side of Chelsea’s squad immediately. Read Chelsea has already examined how Palestra’s arrival offers a tactical clue over Alonso’s defensive plans, and that pressure is now sharpened by market noise around Gusto.

Chelsea can frame the situation in two ways.

One is profit-led. If a club comes close to the reported £75million level, selling a player signed from Lyon for a much lower fee becomes a powerful PSR lever.

The other is football-led. If Alonso sees Gusto as a high-upside wing-back who fits his model, selling him just as the coaching environment becomes more suitable would carry long-term risk.

The complication is Reece James. The captain’s fitness issues, including his current England hamstring concern, mean Chelsea still need genuine right-sided depth.

Palestra may be part of the future, but Gusto is already part of the present. Chelsea have too often needed emergency solutions in that area to treat proven depth lightly.

That is why Read Chelsea’s recent look at James awaiting hamstring scan results matters in this debate. Right-back remains one of the most talented areas of the squad, but also one of the least straightforward.

This is why Gusto’s France rhythm is more valuable than a simple tournament diary entry. Chelsea are watching a player operate inside an elite international camp, learn from a club legend and handle a public transfer valuation that can change his status overnight.

Alonso’s first decision does not have to be final, but it does have to be clear.

If Gusto stays, he needs a defined role early in pre-season and a pathway that makes sense alongside Palestra and James. If Chelsea sell, they need to do it at a number that justifies weakening one of the few squad areas where youth, speed and top-level experience already overlap.

Gusto’s Kante lesson, then, is not just a feel-good Chelsea connection. It is a reminder of the standard Alonso must demand before deciding whether £75million is a price to accept or a warning sign that Chelsea should hold firm.
